criteria.basis: Both have native Windows fixture IPC, argv, process I/O, console cancellation and TUI evidence after X1b, plus native WSL linux-x64 evidence on the frozen pre-X1b builds. G03 demonstrates both Windows-SSH Mode A and a scoped Linux Mode B fixture bridge. Go retains straightforward cgo-free cross-builds, including the observed purego macOS route, but complete macOS SecKey and Windows NCrypt coverage require hand-maintained FFI or cgo. Rust has better typed platform bindings and a smaller macOS adapter, but SDK-dependent macOS linking, zigbuild, thread-per-client Windows pipe work and wrapper-maintenance risks. These offset at 4 each. Neither has validated the full required platform lifecycle/isolation matrix.
criteria.observed_vs_inferred: Observed in retained records: both Windows 71/71, both original linux-x64 139/139, macOS fixture storage/ephemeral SE parity, Linux fixture storage parity, and five Windows pipe checks per language. Inferred: comparative cost of carrying these adapters into production. The G03 bridge is feasibility evidence, not an implemented Go or Rust production bridge; DPAPI/CNG/TPM, cross-user access and lock/restart claims remain unverified.
criteria.strongest_counter: Go can cross-build without a foreign toolchain on its purego route and has go-winio deadlines/overlapped I/O; that could warrant Go 5 versus Rust 4. Conversely, Rust avoids untyped NCrypt/CF calls and, if Iroh ships, can use one implementation language, which could warrant a Rust lead. The macOS Rust wrapper is explicitly looking for a maintainer and has an API that drops OSStatus.

criteria.basis: The common slice is conforming under the accepted rulings after symmetric Windows fixes; neither candidate demonstrates a production authorization/signing core. Rust has compile-time race/exhaustive-state checks in safe code, typed native API signatures and mutable secret buffers. Go has a substantially smaller independently versioned dependency graph, useful built-in binary dependency metadata, reachability scanning and stable native fuzzing. Known logic/signal bugs occur in both; Rust additionally has an observed batch-script-path injection outside the gating argument cases. These make a full-point Rust safety premium unjustified. The X2 recovery finding is assessed primarily under maintenance, not counted again as three security defects.
criteria.observed_vs_inferred: Observed in evidence: no scanner findings in the tested baselines, equal gated conformance, localized Windows data-loss/injection fixes, and the later Rust script-path injection. Compiler guarantees concern specific bug classes, not authorization correctness; expected future benefit is inference. The Go plain Secret Service session is a transport/API fact, not observed unauthorized disclosure. Neither unsafe token counts nor advisory counts measure security incidence.
criteria.strongest_counter: Rust type/race checks and typed platform FFI could justify a point lead for a future concurrent policy runtime. Against that, Rust has about 77–82 normal crates versus 17 Go modules, linked C runtimes, a reported RustSec coverage gap for prospective russh use, and a demonstrated Windows batch-path injection. These could justify a Go lead if production library/control choices do not mitigate them.

criteria.basis: Both tested core prototypes are one executable per target and run without a development toolchain on the tested hosts. X3 gives Go the stronger release path: standard cross-builds, same-host and sampled cross-host identical binaries, embedded dependency buildinfo, artifact SBOM/binary scanning without an extra build step, and a complete GoReleaser snapshot matrix. Rust reproduces on the same host but not across the sampled hosts, requires more linker/remap/toolchain configuration and cargo-auditable for useful binary inventories; cargo-dist Windows was blocked by missing cargo-xwin. T4 cross-review also found swallowed notices-generation failures, confirmed by reading build.sh. Rust remains viable at 3, not a failed distribution approach. Rust wins raw size/CPU, but both slices meet the relevant performance budgets and those small absolute differences do not buy a score point. This row scores the demonstrated core release path; Iroh-enabled architecture is a separate sensitivity case.
criteria.observed_vs_inferred: Observed in records: build hashes, stripped sizes, benchmark samples, snapshot results and tool failures. Independently read here: build.sh only warns on failed notices generation and returns success when any target built. Future pinned-container reproducibility, tag archives, signed installers and native secure-store bundles are not demonstrated. Runtime-size differences for complete V1 are inferred from limited spikes, not measured.
criteria.strongest_counter: A production Rust pipeline using pinned native runners/containers, cargo-auditable and explicit release checks could remove much of this gap. Rust embeds Iroh in one file, whereas Go needs a Rust helper; X5 confirms both build paths. Go archives were not reproducible in snapshot mode, signing/notarization were not executed, and macOS secure-store integration complicates the original SDK-free claim.

criteria.basis: D2 removes personal taste. X2 directly tests comparable changes: all 24 cells pass their intended hidden/harness/unit checks, ordinary reviewers originally find one major in each language, and paired output-token/tool-call ratios are essentially equal. Calibrated review nevertheless finds two repeatable stack pitfalls agents and initial reviewers often miss: Go separate-group recovery in T1 and Bubble Tea wide-character restyling in T3. I give Rust a modest ordinal edge for the tested stack, with low confidence about generalization. T2/T4 and X6 do not justify a blanket Rust productivity or contributor advantage. The T3 finding also affects TUI quality; that correlation is explicit in sensitivity, not treated as another independent language experiment.
criteria.observed_vs_inferred: Recomputed here from results.json: 12/12 cells per language all-build, hidden-all-pass and unit exit 0; 682/635 tool calls and 770583/668620 output tokens; original major totals 1/1. Independent retained probes reproduce the two major families. Inference: these pitfalls predict maintenance cost. T1 recovery is inherited architecture influenced by signal APIs, not better Rust agent implementation; all six introduce the same wrong Running state. The five affected cells are correlated observations from two causes.
criteria.strongest_counter: Equal hidden correctness, near-equal paired effort, equal original major counts, three repetitions per task and only Claude-family implementers support a tie. Calling any wrong job state major makes T1 3 versus 3; calling third-party background stops implausible removes the T1 major split. Go standard tooling and a smaller dependency graph benefit open-source maintenance. Assigning T3 wholly to TUI and discounting the prototype-specific T1 architecture warrants Go 4/Rust 4 and flips the total.

criteria.basis: Both baseline TUIs meet the slice requirements on Unix and native Windows, and both are responsive. The original Bubble Tea out-of-box advantage is outweighed in the tested enhancement by a visible rendering defect: two of three Go T3 cells corrupt destination rows next to wide characters; all Rust cells and the Go full-repaint workaround render those cases correctly. Independent tmux and xterm.js checks reproduce the new defect. Ratatui styled spans avoid the inline-SGR path, so I score the currently evidenced stack Rust 4, Go 3. This is not a language-essential defect or proof of a generally superior UI. Rust still bears its hand-written Unix decoder and crossterm/Windows terminal-cleanup limitations.
criteria.observed_vs_inferred: Observed in retained records: corrupted text in tmux live grids and xterm.js replay, correct controls, and faster Rust benchmark updates. GUI terminal pixels, accessibility/comprehension and operation under a full background workload were not tested. Portability to other terminal implementations is inferred from emitted cursor bytes. The pre-existing R4 status-line defect is terminal-dependent and distinct from the independently reproduced new defect.
criteria.strongest_counter: Go-opus2 avoids the defect with a full repaint, Bubble Tea offers more input/event handling, and Rust required custom Unix decoding to bypass crossterm hazards. A fixed/upgraded renderer could justify equal scores or restoring the original Go lead. Rust Windows external CTRL_C_EVENT leaves the alternate screen active, and existing Rust bidi/zero-width rendering remains a display-spoofing concern.

criteria.basis: Go has the stronger first-party SSH/agent ecosystem and a useful Windows pipe library; Rust has upstream Iroh, typed broad Windows APIs, macOS security wrappers and a working DH Secret Service implementation. X5 closes ring/aws-lc cross-build feasibility and demonstrates a Go supervisor plus Rust helper, so Go is not vetoed by Iroh. X6 does not justify the old blanket 3 versus 5 split when the mandatory product is primarily SSH/agent/platform integration and Iroh may be deferred. Both ecosystems have suitable building blocks with different gaps; neither merits an unqualified 5.
criteria.observed_vs_inferred: Observed in retained X5: all 12 Iroh crypto/target builds succeed, macOS and linux-arm64 loopback exchanges work, Go supervisor and helper lifecycle-on-EOF work. Published third-party maintenance/API/advisory information is snapshot desk research; its fitness for the final product is inference. No maintained adoptable pure-Go Iroh path was demonstrated. Native Windows Iroh, real SSH transport/relay lifecycle and G06 acceptance remain unverified.
criteria.strongest_counter: If G06 retains embedded Iroh for V1, Rust deserves a lead because it removes a second language/artifact/protocol boundary. If Iroh is deferred and ordinary SSH-agent integration dominates, Go deserves a lead. First-party status is not a constraint-enforcement guarantee: X6 reports serious Go agent-constraint advisories, while Rust community agent libraries have a smaller maintainer base.

sensitivity:
Rust leads by 0.05, below one ordinal point in every criterion except ecosystem, where a point exactly ties. This is fragile, not a measured 0.05 productivity advantage. One change at a time: Go +1 or Rust -1 in cross-platform/security moves 0.25 and gives Go a 0.20 lead; in release moves 0.20 and gives Go +0.15; in maintenance moves 0.15 and gives Go +0.10; in TUI moves 0.10 and gives Go +0.05. Go ecosystem 4→5 or Rust 4→3 ties at 3.80 or 3.75 respectively; Rust ecosystem 4→2 flips to Go +0.05. Favorable Rust movements enlarge the lead. No available single whole-point adverse move in the other five rows merely ties.
X2 rubric: excluding the third-party background-stop scenario or counting wrong Running states equally major removes the T1 severity split; T3 remains a reproduced independent defect family. Retaining a modest maintenance lead on T3 alone preserves the main scores, but scoring maintenance 4/4 instead makes Go 3.90 versus Rust 3.80. Treating T3 solely as a TUI/library finding and discounting T1 architecture gives exactly that Go result; the two row advantages must not be called independent corroboration. If only TUI is equalized by raising Go to 4, Go wins 3.85 versus 3.80. Equalizing both rows to 4/4 gives Go 4.00 versus Rust 3.80.
Iroh: main release scores use the demonstrated core build path, while ecosystem weighs SSH and the optional Iroh target together. If Iroh is retained and Rust can ship it embedded, setting release 4/4 and ecosystem Go 4/Rust 5 gives Go 3.75 versus Rust 4.05; actual two-toolchain Go packaging could worsen its release score further. X5 only demonstrates build and loopback feasibility, not G06. If Iroh is deferred and ecosystem becomes Go 4/Rust 3, totals tie 3.75/3.75; equal maintenance then gives Go 3.90 versus Rust 3.75. A proven production Rust release pipeline removing the observed build/inventory gaps raises release 3→4 and Rust to 4.00. A demonstrated inability to meet a hard gate overrides all scores; the unresolved Windows script-path injection cannot be diluted by weighted preferences.

reasons: For the tested Go+Bubble Tea versus Rust+Ratatui stacks, independently reproduced T1 recovery and T3 rendering pitfalls give Rust a modest maintenance/TUI preference under D2. This is two architecture/library causes, not five independent language failures.

Rust supplies useful compiler checks and typed native platform APIs for an agent-maintained concurrent/security product; these are bounded safeguards, not proof of policy correctness. Both viable stacks still need adversarial tests and narrow native adapters.

Rust preserves a native upstream Iroh integration option without a second implementation language/artifact; X5 has now demonstrated its cross-build feasibility. Go release/supply-chain simplicity nearly cancels this preference: the primary weighted margin is just 0.05.
recommendation.strongest_case_for_other: Go is an equally viable close alternative with superior measured core release/rebuild/inventory ergonomics, fewer independently versioned dependencies, strong first-party SSH/agent tools, a good overlapped Windows pipe abstraction and cleaner baseline macOS terminal-signal delivery. X2 hidden success and paired effort tie. Scoring agentic maintenance equal makes Go win; Iroh deferral and a Bubble Tea renderer fix strengthen that choice.
reverse_if: Count maintenance 4/4 after assigning T3 solely to TUI and discounting T1 baseline architecture: Go 3.90, Rust 3.80. Equalizing TUI alone also makes Go win.
Record Iroh deferral and prioritize the required SSH/agent ecosystem: the ecosystem alternative ties the totals even before maintenance adjustments.
Rust cannot demonstrably close the Windows batch-script-path injection or a native isolation/store gate while Go can; a hard-gate failure overrides preferences.
Production-shaped evidence shows Go avoiding the two X2 pitfall families without recurring review burden, or reveals comparable unmeasured Rust maintenance failures.

evidence_concerns: Consequential Windows scope gap: tests/evidence/artifacts/m00-wf8/x1b-review-rust.json reports env-driven command injection through %NAME% in batch script argv[0] and wrong-file execution. X1b 71/71 tests ordinary argument escaping, not that path. The reviewer called it minor because pre-existing/outside the patch; causal provenance does not reduce product impact. D3 fixes existing rulings but does not supply the missing argv[0] interpretation. Security remains uncertain; do not describe Rust Windows launches as universally injection-safe.

X2 attribution overreach: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/RESULTS.md §5.3–§6 says both major families trace to the Go stack. tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/t1-calibration/verify/README.md shows all six implementers introduce the same Running-state regression and Rust recovery executes none of their new T1 logic. Go recovery was avoidably wrong within the standard-library model. This supports a tested-architecture pitfall, not a causal claim that Go agents code less reliably or Rust makes job control correct.

X2 rubric sensitivity and dependence: five affected Go cells versus zero Rust are two correlated cause families, not twelve independent success/failure trials. The conditional Fisher p≈0.02 in tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/RESULTS.md is explicitly hypothetical and must not be promoted to significance. T1 severity depends on plausible third-party background stops and what counts as normal recovery; all six have wrong job states. New regressions and larger pre-existing Rust debt are accounted differently. TUI and maintenance row use of the same T3 finding is correlated; sensitivity quantifies removing it from maintenance.

Probe correction matters: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/t1-calibration/README.md correction and verify/README.md supersede claims that Darwin ^C does nothing. Default-disposition ^C kills the Go job (130); the earlier result inherited ignored SIGINT from the probe launcher. Linux no-normal-recovery and Rust ^Z+fg completion remain reproduced. Do not copy the stale appendices without the correction. A generic tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/RESULTS.md claim that both baselines match plain exec in P1 must be narrowed: base-Go Darwin SIGSTOP exits 255, whereas its SIGTSTP and Linux cases mirror stops.

Status/provenance wording: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/RESULTS.md marks the two major families verified, while individual cross-review/T3/verify/README.md and t1-calibration/verify/README.md label their own records implemented_unverified pending another rerun. There are genuinely separate retained reproduction runs, so the facts carry weight, but not every calibrated minor/pre-existing rating is independently verified. Go patch-version changes explain several nonidentical binaries; source-equivalent probes are not original-byte verification.

Hidden-test ceiling and mutation gap: all 24 X2 cells pass intended hidden tests, and original reviewers have 1/1 majors. tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/cross-review/T4/README.md shows mutants without the opened-file check pass hidden T4 despite SEED.md saying otherwise. Cross-review catches it, and actual fixes retain the check, but hidden-all-pass is not robust regression proof. T3 136/139 is deliberate replacement of three K9-coupled checks, not permission to ignore unrelated NO_COLOR/latency failures; the T3 pack separately checks these properties.

Release false-green: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x2/cross-review/T4/README.md reports notices generation fails on every Rust rebuild while build.sh exits 0. Reading prototypes/rust/build.sh confirms notice failure only warns and the final exit condition requires any, not all, target to build. The recorded per-target manifests support these experiments actual four-target builds; shell exit 0 alone proves neither complete matrix nor release-compliant notices.

Clean-machine and native-scope gap: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x1/RESULTS.md uses restricted PATH on an owner/developer Windows host and env -i on existing hosts, not clean signed installations. macOS X4 ad-hoc bundles fail Gatekeeper; provisioned persistence/lock tests are blocked. docs/research/g03-windows-wsl.md §0 has 11 verified WSL records with remaining account/distribution/lock/UAC blockers, and native Windows has six fully verified records plus partial/blocked records. Native linux-x64 139/139 applies to the pre-X1b binaries; post-X1b review executed only darwin/linux-arm64. Do not relabel all G03 or every post-X1b architecture verified.

Go Windows identity claim was overbroad and corrected: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x1/RESULTS.md and x1-review/host-runs/rv-ps51-a/review-probes.json distinguish anonymous impersonation failure from successful process-token identification used by Win32-OpenSSH. This is not an observed test against the owners actual agent. X4 expected-foreign-SID refusal uses the same account against a deliberately mismatched expected SID; it does not establish DACL denial against an actual foreign account.

X3 counting/tool limits: Go module counts and Rust crate counts differ in granularity; unsafe grep is target-filtered only for Go, Rust has whole-source upper bounds, and neither count includes its whole standard/runtime surface. Zero CVEs is DB/tool-specific, not a security pass. Rust cross-host hash differences are real but their cause remains undiagnosed; cargo-dist missing a tool/default configuration problems are remediable pipeline issues, not language impossibility. Archive/tag-release/signing checks were not completed for either candidate.

X5 overclaim: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x5/RESULTS.md says a real Go helper makes the measured payload gap at least this large. This is not a proven lower bound: Rust embedded production integration would also gain protocol/lifecycle code, features/profiles differ, and Go can redesign the core. 12 successful builds and loopback exchanges close only the build risk, not Windows Iroh runtime, native x64 networking, ordinary SSH, relay/discovery/restart or G06. X1 Windows prototype execution does not close X5 binaries.

X6 evidence quality: tests/evidence/artifacts/g02-r4/x6/RESULTS.md compares different repositories/tasks per language, reuses Multilingual across studies, includes old/different models, and gets some facts through an LLM fetcher; PDFs are not retained. Its broad limitations claim of 22–43 tasks per language omits the much larger Multi-SWE-bench sample shown in its own table. Contributor/advisory counts and active release snapshots are not comparative maintainability/safety proof. The russh advisory gap concerns a prospective package absent from the current prototype; this review did not live-refresh the source snapshots.

Scope and licensing: docs/decisions/0002-language-tui-distribution.md predates round 4 and contains stale no-host/open-decision language; its §10 D2 personal-ergonomics question is superseded by the recorded owner ruling. tests/evidence/g02-measurements.json is slice data, not full-runtime/72-hour-soak evidence. X3 license tools omit standard/CRT components and ignore the UNLICENSED root; Rust offline notice failure weakens blanket notice claims. X4 file-keychain deprecated APIs and ephemeral SE results do not establish persistent hardware custody or locked signing in either language.
owner_questions: D4 completion boundary: does the owner consider the executed native Windows/WSL feasibility sufficient to record D1, or must the already-listed G03 second-account/distribution/restart/host-lock and real-upstream tests finish first? The current records do not establish full G03/V1 support. This is an interpretation of the existing deferral, not a request to change D3.

Windows authority/contract ambiguity for the orchestrator or owner: does §9.6 no argument byte include the batch script path argv[0]? Independent Rust review observed injection there.
